paper_context.research_question: Can annotated event-argument information be exploited explicitly via supervised attention mechanisms to improve event detection (trigger identification and classification) compared to existing pipeline and joint approaches on ACE 2005?
main_claims: Explicitly supervising attention with annotated argument information improves event detection performance over unsupervised attention and prior state-of-the-art systems on ACE 2005.
Two strategies to construct gold attention (S1: only arguments; S2: arguments + surrounding words) are effective, with S2 achieving higher recall and overall best F1 while S1 yields higher precision.
Augmenting training data with automatically extracted FrameNet events further improves recall and F1 for the supervised-attention models.

The limited gains for ED in prior joint ED+AE models stem from imbalanced supervision and the common practice of not using argument information when pre-predicting triggers; supervised attention provides a direct way to use arguments for ED.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Trigger detection/classification F1 on ACE 2005 (primary metric)
Precision and recall breakdown (to compare S1 vs S2 behavior)
Ablation comparing supervised vs unsupervised attention and entity-only attention
Robustness to data augmentation (using FrameNet) and sensitivity to hyperparameters like λ and attention window
Qualitative analysis showing attention focusing on argument words (interpretability)

extracted_claims.claim_text: Explicitly supervising attention with annotated argument information improves event detection performance (trigger identification and classification) compared to unsupervised attention and prior state-of-the-art systems on ACE 2005.
evidence: Abstract: "Experimental results show that our approach advances state-of-the-arts and achieves the best F1 score on ACE 2005 dataset."
Introduction: description of supervised attention using annotated arguments (lines ~150-200).
Section 4.3, Table 3: ANN-S2 reported P=78.0, R=66.3, F1=71.7 vs. baselines including Liu's FN-Based (F1=70.7) and others; authors state ANN-S2 achieves best performance and t-test p<=0.05.
uncertainty_flags: Reported comparison relies on a specific train/dev/test split (randomly selected 30 dev, 40 test newswire docs) rather than the full standard ACE predefined splits; reproducibility depends on exact split.
Statistical test claimed (t-test p<=0.05) but details (number of runs, variance, paired/unpaired test, metric used) are not fully specified.
Exact hyperparameter tuning and potential model selection on test set not fully detailed; potential risk of optimistic estimates.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Two strategies to construct gold attention (S1: only argument words; S2: arguments plus surrounding words modeled by a Gaussian) are effective, with S2 achieving higher recall and overall best F1 while S1 yields higher precision.
extracted_claims.section_anchor: Section 3.2.2 (Constructing Gold Attention Vectors); Section 4.3 (experimental comparison, Table 3)
evidence: Section 3.2.2: Definition of S1 and S2; S2 uses gaussian distribution with window size and parameters (µ=0, σ=1, window=3).
Table 3: ANN-S1 reported P=81.4, R=62.4, F1=70.8; ANN-S2 P=78.0, R=66.3, F1=71.7; authors' interpretation lines ~633-674.
uncertainty_flags: Only two S1/S2 variants are evaluated; other parameterizations of S2 (µ, σ, window) not extensively explored in reported results.
No per-class or example-level analysis shown to verify that S1 precision gains stem specifically from argument-only focus versus other confounds.
Unclear whether S1/S2 hyperparameters (e.g., λ) were optimized comparably and whether results are robust to such tuning.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Augmenting training data with automatically extracted FrameNet events further improves recall and F1 for the supervised-attention models and the baseline.
evidence: Section 4.4: authors describe using Liu et al. (2016a) FrameNet-derived events, processing to map frame elements to arguments and using RPI system to produce entity labels.
Table 4: ANN baseline F1 increases from 64.6 to 66.2 with FrameNet; ANN-S1 from 70.8 to 70.9; ANN-S2 from 71.7 to 71.9; reported increases in recall for augmented systems.
uncertainty_flags: FrameNet-derived events lack original entity/argument annotations and are automatically processed; noise level and label mismatch may vary and are not quantified.
Gains are modest for supervised systems (ANN-S1/S2) and could be within variability; statistical testing for augmentation effects not reported.
Details of how FrameNet examples were balanced or weighted versus ACE examples (e.g., mixing ratio, shuffling) are not fully specified.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Reason joint methods underperform on ED
extracted_claims.claim_text: Limited gains for ED in prior joint ED+AE models stem from imbalanced supervision (many more argument annotations than triggers) and the common practice of not using argument information when pre-predicting triggers; supervised attention provides a direct way to use arguments for ED.
evidence: Intro: authors note ACE has ~9800 arguments vs ~5300 triggers and argue that joint models' combined losses may favor AE; also claim pre-prediction phases in joint models often ignore arguments.
Related work: authors contrast their explicit argument use to prior joint methods and point to Table 1 showing ED performance differences between pipeline and joint systems.
uncertainty_flags: The causal link (imbalance -> ED underperformance) is argued but not directly tested empirically in the manuscript (no controlled ablation on loss weighting or pre-prediction practices).

The claim about implementation practices in prior work (not using arguments when pre-predicting triggers) is stated generally but may not hold for all joint approaches; evidence is limited to cited papers without detailed re-implementation.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Unsupervised attention is ineffective without augmentation
extracted_claims.claim_text: Unsupervised attention mechanisms perform poorly for ED on ACE 2005 (baseline ANN F1=64.6), likely because ACE training data is insufficient to train precise attentions in an unsupervised manner; data augmentation (FrameNet) helps the unsupervised baseline.
evidence: Section 4.3 observation: authors report ANN baseline unexpectedly poor (P=73.2, R=57.9, F1=64.6) and hypothesize data sparsity as reason (citing Zhu et al. 2014; Liu et al. 2016a).
Section 4.4 Table 4: ANN +FrameNet F1 improves to 66.2.
uncertainty_flags: Other reasons for ANN baseline weakness (architectural choices, hyperparameters, implementation differences) are possible but not ruled out.
Improvement with FrameNet is shown, but the extent to which it addresses attention learning specifically (vs. general supervised signal) is not isolated.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Training the attention mechanism jointly with the event detector using a mean squared error loss between machine attention and constructed gold attention (weighted by λ) yields effective models for ED.
extracted_claims.section_anchor: Section 3.2.2 (Jointly Training ED and Attention); Equation 8 and 9; Section 4.3 hyperparameter choices
evidence: Equations 8 and 9 define D(θ)=sum squared error between α* and α and joint loss J'(θ)=J(θ)+λD(θ).
Section 4.3: reported λ values used (ANN-S1 λ=1.0; ANN-S2 λ=5.0) and improved results for these settings.
uncertainty_flags: Choice of squared error as attention loss (vs. KLD or cross-entropy) is not compared empirically; effectiveness may depend on scale and normalization of attention vectors.
λ values appear chosen per strategy but broader sensitivity analysis is not reported.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Annotated arguments in ACE training data are accurate and sufficiently informative to construct reliable gold attention vectors for supervising attention.
supporting_evidence: Authors use ACE annotated arguments to build gold attention vectors (S1/S2) and report gains when supervised by these vectors (Sections 3.2.2, 4.3).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If ACE argument annotations are noisy, incomplete, or not predictive of triggers, supervised attention could learn misleading signals, reducing generalization and inflating apparent gains on ACE while failing on other data.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Entity type embeddings (from ACE entity annotations or RPI system for FrameNet) are informative and consistently mapped between ACE and FrameNet-augmented data.
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: Section 3.1.2 (Entity Type Embedding Table); Section 4.4 (processing FrameNet events)
supporting_evidence: Model uses entity type embeddings alongside word embeddings in CRL; FrameNet events are processed to obtain entity labels via RPI system before augmentation.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If entity typing is inconsistent, noisy, or mismatched across ACE and augmented FrameNet examples, learned representations may be corrupted, weakening attention supervision and classifier performance.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The random split used (30 dev, 40 test newswire, 529 train) is comparable to prior work and does not bias results in favor of the proposed method.
supporting_evidence: Authors state they followed evaluation of Li et al. (2013); Chen et al. (2015); Liu et al. (2016b) by selecting 30 dev and 40 test documents.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the split differs in systematic ways or was tuned, comparisons to prior systems could be invalid; reported improvements might be due to data selection rather than method.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Square error between gold and machine attention is an appropriate loss for supervising attention distributions and interacts well with softmax-produced attention.
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: Section 3.2.2 (Jointly Training ED and Attention); Equations 2, 8-9
supporting_evidence: Authors select MSE (Equation 8) as attention loss and show improved downstream metrics when combined with classification loss.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: MSE may not be the best divergence for distributions (compared to KL), potentially leading to suboptimal attention training or sensitivity to scaling/normalization.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Using a Gaussian centered on argument positions (S2) properly captures useful contextual cues and the selected hyperparameters (µ=0, σ=1, window=3) are appropriate.
supporting_evidence: S2 is defined using a gaussian g(d, µ, σ) with µ=0, σ=1 and window=3; experiments show ANN-S2 has higher recall and best F1.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the gaussian shape/window poorly models useful context for some event types, S2 could add noise and harm generalization; sensitivity to µ/σ/window not reported.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: FrameNet-derived events, after selecting core frame elements and adding entity annotations via RPI, are sufficiently similar to ACE events to be useful as augmentation.
supporting_evidence: Authors follow Liu et al. (2016a) to use FrameNet events and map frame elements to arguments and use RPI system for entity labels; results show modest improvements.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If FrameNet frames are not well aligned to ACE event types or RPI entity labeling introduces errors, augmented data may introduce label noise that hurts rather than helps learning.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The implementation details (architecture, optimization, hyperparameters) are comparable to baselines and do not introduce confounding advantages.
supporting_evidence: Authors specify architecture: 3-layer ANN, embedding dims, hidden sizes, Adadelta, dropout rate, L2, batch size; compared against prior reported numbers in literature.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If differing preprocessing, tokenization, or other implementation choices favor the proposed method, comparative claims could be confounded.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Attention supervision is applied during training only (except for ANN-Gold systems which use gold attention at test), and learned attention generalizes at test when only prediction-time inputs are available.
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: Section 3.2.2 (Joint training) and Section 4.2 (ANN-Gold systems described as using gold attention in both training and testing)
supporting_evidence: ANN-S1/ANN-S2 are described as trained with gold attention supervision and then used at test using learned attention; ANN-Gold1/2 are explicitly said to use gold attentions in testing for correctness checks.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If learned attention fails to approximate gold attention at test time (because gold requires gold argument spans unavailable at test), supervised gains observed during training may not transfer, or reported comparisons using ANN-Gold systems could be optimistic if used to motivate approach.

argument_focus: Whether explicit supervision of attention with argument-derived gold vectors causally improves ED, beyond general benefits of added supervision.
The robustness and sensitivity of S1 vs S2 construction (parameters µ, σ, window, λ).
The quality and compatibility of FrameNet-derived augmentation after automatic entity labeling.
Comparability of experimental protocol (data splits, preprocessing, baseline reimplementations) with prior work.

Empirical claim of state-of-the-art F1 on ACE 2005 with ANN-S2.
Demonstration that FrameNet-derived augmented data provides additional gains when combined with supervised attention.

Ablation of attention loss choice (MSE vs KL vs cross-entropy) and λ sensitivity sweep for both S1 and S2.
Per-class precision/recall to see which event types benefit most from argument supervision.
Analysis comparing learned attention maps to gold attention for held-out examples (quantify alignment).

Quantify noise introduced by FrameNet processing: percentage of mismatched or low-quality mappings and effect on performance as a function of FN data amount.

Experimental split selection procedure described as 'followed' but exact seed/split not provided; reproducibility risk.
FrameNet processing pipeline (RPI labeling) may introduce unreported noise; mapping from frames to ACE types is not fully detailed.
chaining_notes: Downstream reviewers should (1) attempt to reproduce reported numbers with identical preprocessing and split or request the split used; (2) test sensitivity to λ, attention-loss formulation, and S2 gaussian parameters; (3) compare supervised-attention to other explicit ways of using argument annotations (e.g., features, multi-task) to isolate mechanism; (4) evaluate learned attention alignment to gold argument spans quantitatively; (5) audit FrameNet augmentation quality and its marginal contribution when controlling for data quantity versus label noise.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript motivates using annotated event-argument information to explicitly supervise neural attention for event detection (ED). It proposes two ways to construct gold attention vectors from argument annotations (S1: argument-only; S2: arguments + Gaussian-smoothed surrounding words), trains a joint loss that adds MSE between model attention and gold attention weighted by λ, and shows improved F1 on ACE 2005 vs. unsupervised-attention baseline and several prior systems. It also experiments with augmenting ACE training data using automatically derived FrameNet events. The paper's reasoning chain is: (1) arguments are informative for disambiguating triggers; (2) existing pipeline/joint approaches underuse argument info for ED; (3) supervising attention to focus on arguments should direct the model to exploit that signal; (4) two construction strategies trade precision/recall; (5) augmentation with FrameNet mitigates data sparsity and helps attention learning. Empirical support (Tables 2-4) aligns with these steps, but the causal claims that supervised attention, rather than other confounds (preprocessing, split, architecture/hyperparameters, loss choices), produce the gains are not fully isolated. Missing details or limited ablations (statistical testing details, multiple seeds, alternative attention losses, quantitative alignment between learned and gold attentions, and controlled comparisons to other explicit uses of argument info) leave parts of the argument vulnerable to alternative explanations. The paper is coherent and plausible; its strongest logical link is that gold-attention-oracle experiments (ANN-Gold1/2) show argument information can yield large gains when available at test time. The weakest links are the untested causal attribution that joint models fail ED because of loss imbalance and that the specific MSE+λ choice is optimal; both are argued but not empirically resolved.
logical_argument_graph: Problem statement: ED sometimes misclassifies ambiguous triggers; annotated arguments can disambiguate triggers (Introduction -> motivating examples).
Observation: Prior pipeline methods ignore arguments; joint ED+AE methods improve AE more than ED (Table 1) (Introduction -> Related Work).
Hypothesis: Directly supervising attention with argument-derived gold attention will enable ED models to exploit argument cues and improve performance (Sections 3.2.2 and 3.1.3).
Operationalization: Define two gold-attention construction strategies S1 (arguments only) and S2 (arguments + gaussian-weighted neighbors) (Section 3.2.2).
Model: Learn attention and ED jointly with classification loss J and attention MSE loss D weighted by λ => J' = J + λD (Equations 7-9).
Empirical test A (oracle): ANN-Gold1/2 (use gold attention at train+test) demonstrate large gains showing argument information is sufficient if available (Section 4.2, Table 2).
Empirical test B (learned): ANN-S1/ANN-S2 (train with gold-attention supervision, test with learned attention) outperform unsupervised-attention ANN and prior SOTA on ACE 2005 (Section 4.3, Table 3).
Analysis: S1 yields higher precision, S2 yields higher recall (Table 3 and interpretation) — supporting the design-choice claim about tradeoffs (Section 4.3).

Augmentation: Use FrameNet-derived events (processed by RPI) to augment training data; modest additional gains especially in recall indicate data-sparsity limitation for unsupervised attention (Section 4.4, Table 4).

Broader claim: Supervised attention addresses a key reason joint methods underperform on ED (imbalanced supervision and pre-prediction practices), offering a direct way to use arguments for ED (Introduction, Related Work).

strengths.title: Clear causal hypothesis linking arguments to attention
strengths.description: Paper articulates a concrete mechanism (supervising attention with argument-derived gold vectors) tying annotated arguments to improved trigger classification.
evidence: Sections 3.2.2 and 3.1.3 explicitly define gold attention construction and joint training loss.
ANN-Gold1/2 oracle experiments demonstrate that argument-focused attention is sufficient to improve ED.

strengths.title: Two interpretable attention-construction strategies
strengths.description: Authors present two conceptually simple strategies (S1 and S2) that have complementary precision/recall behavior, enabling interpretable trade-offs.
evidence: Detailed definitions of S1 (argument-only) and S2 (gaussian-smoothed) in Section 3.2.2 and empirical Table 3 showing precision/recall differences.

strengths.title: Empirical improvement over several baselines
strengths.description: Reported results place the supervised-attention system above multiple prior methods on ACE 2005 under comparable split choices.

concerns.title: Reproducibility risk: dataset split and randomness
concerns.description: The paper follows a randomized split (30 dev, 40 test) referenced to prior work but does not provide the exact seed or concrete split; without these specifics reproduction and fair comparison may be compromised.
evidence: Section 4.1 describes random selection of 30 dev and 40 test documents but no seed or file lists are provided in manuscript.
Shared analysis notes comparisons rely on this split and reproducibility depends on exact split.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide the exact list of document IDs used for train/dev/test splits or release the split files and training/test scripts; report results averaged over multiple random splits/seeds with standard deviations.

concerns.title: Statistical testing and run variance missing
concerns.description: The paper reports a t-test claim (p<=0.05) but omits how many runs, which metric distribution or whether tests are paired; single-run results without variance diminish confidence in significance.
evidence: Section 4.3 states 'we perform a t-test (p<=0.05)' but provides no test details; Tables show single-point P/R/F1 numbers without stddev.
Shared_analysis flags missing test details and number of runs.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report mean and standard deviation across multiple random seeds (e.g., 5-10 runs); specify paired/unpaired t-test, test statistic, and apply appropriate test (e.g., paired bootstrap) over test examples or runs.

concerns.title: Insufficient ablation to isolate attention supervision effect
concerns.description: Improvements may stem from additional supervision rather than the attention mechanism per se; the manuscript lacks controlled comparisons to alternative ways of using argument annotations (e.g., indicator features, multi-task losses, or concatenated argument embeddings).
evidence: Shared_analysis recommends a controlled test: same supervision amount but not via attention (e.g., argument indicator features) to check whether attention-specific supervision drives gains.
Paper presents ANN-ENT (entity averaging) but not other explicit-argument baselines.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add an ablation that uses the same gold-argument supervision but injects it as explicit features or a multi-task objective (predict argument presence/roles) to compare with supervised-attention; measure whether attention-supervision uniquely improves ED.

concerns.title: Choice of attention loss and λ unexamined
concerns.description: The model uses MSE between attention vectors and picks λ values per strategy, but no comparison to other divergences (KL, cross-entropy) or sensitivity analysis for λ is provided; this leaves the optimization rationale under-specified.
evidence: Equations 8-9 define MSE; Section 4.3 reports λ=1.0 for S1 and λ=5.0 for S2 without sweeps.
Shared_analysis flags lack of comparison between MSE and KL and insufficient λ sensitivity.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report experiments comparing MSE to KL and cross-entropy as attention loss and provide λ sensitivity plots (F1 vs λ) for S1 and S2 to show robustness.

concerns.title: FrameNet augmentation processing and noise unquantified
concerns.description: The FrameNet-derived augmentation requires mapping frame elements to arguments and using automatic entity labeling (RPI); the paper does not quantify mapping quality or noise, nor the mixing strategy for FN vs ACE data.
evidence: Section 4.4 describes selecting core frame elements and using RPI for entities but provides no precision/recall or error analysis of these automatic labels.
Table 4 shows small gains for supervised models, which may be due to quantity or noise rather than mechanism.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide basic diagnostic statistics for the FN-ACE mapping (e.g., fraction of FN examples with successful entity labeling, estimated label noise) and document the mixing ratio and sampling procedure for combining FN and ACE during training.

concerns.title: Lack of quantitative attention alignment analysis
concerns.description: The interpretability claim (that learned attention focuses on argument words) is supported qualitatively but lacks quantitative alignment metrics comparing learned attention to gold attention on held-out data.
evidence: Paper shows ANN-Gold oracle performance and describes attention behavior, but no alignment statistics (e.g., cosine similarity, AUC for argument-word ranking) are reported.
Shared_analysis suggests evaluating learned attention maps to gold attention quantitatively.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report alignment metrics between learned attention α and gold α* over the test set (e.g., average MSE, KL divergence, top-k overlap), and include per-class breakdowns to show where alignment correlates with performance gains.

alternative_interpretations: Performance gains may result primarily from additional supervised signal (explicit argument supervision) irrespective of attention architecture; supervised attention could be acting as a proxy for injecting argument indicators, and simpler feature-based injections might yield similar gains.
Implementation differences (embedding training corpus, hyperparameter tuning, tokenization, batch size, or regularization) compared to baselines may explain part of the reported improvement.

Oracle experiments (ANN-Gold1/2) show argument information is useful, but learned-attention gains could stem from better regularization or λ-weighted joint training acting as auxiliary loss, not necessarily from attention focusing on arguments.
transparency_notes: Provide exact data split files and seed to enable reproduction.
Share code for gold-attention construction, training (including λ, learning curves), and FrameNet processing (mapping and RPI usage).
Report per-class P/R/F1, standard deviations across multiple runs, and attention-alignment metrics to increase transparency.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: Although supervised attention as a concept has precedents (e.g., Mi et al. 2016), applying it to ED using annotated argument-derived gold vectors and the two proposed construction strategies S1/S2 is a novel adaptation; novelty does not imply correctness — empirical controls are needed to rule out confounds.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If ACE argument annotations are accurate and consistently mapped to gold-attention vectors (A1 holds), supervised-attention should guide the model toward informative context words and yield replicable gains.

If MSE is a reasonable divergence for the attention vector normalization used and λ is tuned robustly per strategy, joint training will properly trade-off classification and attention alignment (A4 holds).
If FrameNet-derived examples are mapped with sufficient quality and mixing with ACE training data is balanced, augmentation will increase recall and help unsupervised attention converge (A6 holds).
If differences from prior baselines are not driven by preprocessing or split choices and the code is matched for hyperparameters, the reported improvements will persist across multiple seeds.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Supervised attention is an existing idea (applied in NMT etc.), but using argument annotations to construct gold attentions for ED and the S1/S2 constructions are domain-specific adaptations that are useful and not previously reported in the same way.
evidence: Mi et al. (2016) is cited for supervised attention; manuscript adapts idea specifically for event detection and argument annotation use.
uncertainty_flags: Extent to which S1/S2 are novel vs straightforward adaptations is moderate; novelty is real but incremental.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Reported empirical gains on ACE 2005 and oracle experiments suggest practical benefit; however, the robustness of gains requires additional ablations and reproducibility checks.
evidence: Table 3 shows ANN-S2 improves F1 over several baselines; ANN-Gold experiments show argument information is sufficient to improve ED.
uncertainty_flags: Single-run reporting and lack of variance/statistical details reduce confidence in impact magnitude.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident that the proposed supervised-attention approach is a valid and promising method to exploit argument annotations for ED (evidence: oracle and learned experiments show gains). However, reproducibility concerns (split/single-run reporting), missing ablations to isolate mechanisms (alternative supervision injection, attention-loss choices), and unquantified augmentation noise reduce certainty about the claimed magnitude and generality of improvements.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes supervising the attention mechanism of an ANN-based event detector using argument annotations from ACE 2005. Two procedures to construct gold attention vectors are proposed: S1 (argument tokens only) and S2 (arguments plus nearby words via a Gaussian kernel). The attention loss (MSE between machine and gold attention) is combined with the classification loss using trade-off weight λ. Experiments on ACE 2005 (train: 529 docs, dev: 30, test: 40 newswire docs) show improvements: ANN baseline (unsupervised attention) F1=64.6; ANN-S1 F1=70.8; ANN-S2 F1=71.7. Augmenting training with FrameNet-derived events produces small additional recall and F1 increases. Authors argue that supervised attention enables direct use of argument information, explaining prior joint models' limited ED gains. Key empirical claims are supported by tables (Tables 2–4) though important experimental and statistical details are incomplete.
logical_argument_graph: A1: Argument annotations contain signal useful for disambiguating triggers -> motivates supervising attention towards arguments.
Model design: compute attention from candidate and context; create gold attention from ACE arguments (S1, S2); jointly train classification loss + λ*MSE(attention).
Prediction: supervised attention will focus representation on argument-aware context, improving trigger classification.
Empirical test: compare ANN (unsupervised attention), ANN-ENT, ANN-Gold variants, ANN-S1, ANN-S2 on ACE 2005 split -> ANN-S2 yields highest F1.
Augmentation test: add FrameNet-derived events (with automatic entity labeling) -> modest further gains, especially recall.

Conclusion: explicit attention supervision with argument signals causally improves ED relative to unsupervised attention and prior baselines; S1/S2 give a precision/recall tradeoff; augmentation helps.

Section 4.2/4.3: comparisons against prior methods (Li 2013; Liu 2016a/b; Nguyen 2016) with reported metrics.

Statistical significance claimed (t-test p<=0.05) but test details (number of runs, variance, paired/unpaired) are not provided.

evidence: Section 3.2.2 describes S1 and S2 construction (Gaussian window in S2).
uncertainty_flags: Only one parameterization of S2 (µ=0, σ=1, window=3) is reported; no sensitivity analysis on µ/σ/window shown.
No per-event-type breakdown to confirm that S1's higher precision is due to better argument focus rather than random variation.

Section 4.4 describes processing FN frames to core elements and using RPI system for entity labels.

Quality/noise of automatically labeled FN examples (entity mapping errors, frame-to-ACE mapping) is not quantified.

identified_claims.claim_text: Limited gains for ED in prior joint ED+AE models stem from imbalanced supervision and the common practice of not using argument information when pre-predicting triggers; supervised attention provides a direct way to use arguments for ED.
evidence: Authors note ACE has ~9800 arguments vs ~5300 triggers and describe implementation practices of joint methods pre-predicting triggers without argument signals.
Table 1 compares pipeline vs joint ED/AE performance showing joint methods mainly improve AE.
uncertainty_flags: Causal link between class imbalance and ED underperformance is argued qualitatively but not tested (no controlled ablation on loss weighting or training schedules).
The assertion about implementation practices of prior work (not using arguments in pre-prediction) is general and not empirically validated across cited methods.

identified_claims.claim_text: Unsupervised attention mechanisms perform poorly for ED on ACE 2005 (baseline ANN F1=64.6), likely because ACE training data is insufficient to train precise attentions in an unsupervised manner; data augmentation (FrameNet) helps the unsupervised baseline.
evidence: Section 4.3 reports ANN F1=64.6 and hypothesizes data sparsity as the cause.
Table 4: ANN +FrameNet F1=66.2 (improvement).
uncertainty_flags: Alternative explanations for ANN baseline weakness (implementation, hyperparameters, preprocessing) are not ruled out.
No ablation demonstrates attention weights specifically improved after augmentation (alignment between learned attention and gold not quantified).

identified_claims.claim_text: Training the attention mechanism jointly with the event detector using a mean squared error loss between machine attention and constructed gold attention (weighted by λ) yields effective models for ED.
evidence: Equations define D(θ) as sum squared error and joint loss J'(θ)=J(θ)+λD(θ).
Reported λ choices (λ=1.0 for S1, λ=5.0 for S2) and improved ED metrics for those settings.

No systematic sweep of λ is reported to show robustness of the joint objective to weighting.

strengths.title: Clear causal mechanism linking arguments to attention
strengths.description: The paper provides a transparent rationale: annotated arguments identify informative context words; supervising attention to focus on these should produce representations better suited to trigger classification.
evidence: Intro motivation and formalization in Section 3.2.2: construction of gold attentions from arguments (S1, S2).
Empirical gain when training with gold attentions (ANN-Gold1/2) indicates arguments are informative.

strengths.title: Simple, implementable supervised-attention training regime
strengths.description: The joint loss (classification + λ*MSE on attention) is straightforward to implement and integrates cleanly with standard ANN training pipelines, enabling reproducibility if experimental details are provided.
evidence: Equations 7–9 define objective; Section 3 and 4 specify network layers, embedding dims, optimizer (Adadelta), dropout, and λ examples.

strengths.title: Empirical ablation that isolates argument usage
strengths.description: The authors include systems that separately test unsupervised attention (ANN), entity-based averaging (ANN-ENT), gold-attention at test (ANN-Gold1/2), and supervised attention (ANN-S1/S2), which helps trace where improvements originate.
evidence: Definitions in Section 4.2 and comparison results in Table 2/Table 3 showing performance differences among these variants.

strengths.description: Paper examines whether external automatically-extracted event data helps, and reports its impact on baseline and supervised models, which is useful for assessing data-scarcity claims.
evidence: Section 4.4 describes processing FN frames to core elements, using RPI system for entity labeling, and Table 4 provides results with +FrameNet.

concerns.title: Reproducibility risk from unspecified data split and seeds
concerns.description: The paper follows a random split (30 dev, 40 test) but does not publish the exact split, random seed, or share code/splits; reproducing the results and comparing fairly to prior work depends on these details.
evidence: Section 4.1: 'randomly selected 30 articles ... and subsequently conducted a blind test on a separate set of 40 ACE 2005 newswire documents' but no split file or seed provided.
Shared analysis notes that comparability to prior work depends on exact split.

concerns.title: Insufficient statistical reporting
concerns.description: A t-test p<=0.05 is claimed but the paper omits crucial details: number of experimental runs, whether the test is paired, metric distribution, and which comparisons were tested.

No run-to-run variance, standard deviation, or seed-averaged results are reported.

concerns.description: The ANN baseline performs markedly worse than some prior reported systems; it's unclear whether this stems from attention choice, architectural differences, preprocessing, or hyperparameters, which undermines claims about supervised attention efficacy.
evidence: Table 3: ANN baseline F1=64.6 while several published baselines (Liu's PSL, Skip-CNN) report 69–71 F1.
Paper hypothesizes data sparsity but does not rule out other causes.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide detailed preprocessing/tokenization, replicate at least one strong baseline implementation (e.g., Skip-CNN) under identical conditions, or tune ANN until it matches earlier reported baselines to isolate the effect of supervised attention.

concerns.title: Limited sensitivity analysis on attention construction and λ
concerns.description: Only one S2 parameterization and single λ values per strategy are reported. The effect of Gaussian parameters (µ, σ, window) and λ sensitivity are not explored; results may be dependent on these choices.
evidence: Section 4.1 sets µ=0, σ=1, window=3; Section 4.3 uses λ=1 (S1) and λ=5 (S2) but no sweep results are shown.
Shared analysis suggests ablation of λ and attention loss form as key evaluation targets.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include λ sweeps (e.g., {0.1,1,5,10}), alternative attention-loss functions (KL, CE), and S2 parameter sensitivity (different σ and windows) with results on dev set; report how stable gains are.

concerns.title: No quantitative alignment between learned and gold attention at test
concerns.description: The paper asserts interpretability (attention focuses on arguments) but does not quantify alignment between learned attention vectors and constructed gold attentions on held-out data.
evidence: ANN-Gold systems use gold attention at test; ANN-S systems rely on learned attention. No metrics such as cosine similarity, KL, or top-k overlap between learned/gold attentions reported.
Shared analysis lists 'evaluate learned attention maps to gold attention' as needed.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report distributional alignment metrics (e.g., average cosine similarity or KL) between learned attention and gold attention on the test/dev sets; provide qualitative examples illustrating successes and failures.

concerns.title: FrameNet augmentation pipeline under-specified and unquantified
concerns.description: Processing FN frames to ACE-like events relies on automatic entity labeling (RPI) and mapping to core elements, but the error rate or label mismatch introduced is not measured; marginal gains could be contaminated by noise or differ by event type.
evidence: Section 4.4: 'we use events published by Liu et al. (2016a) ... lack both argument and entity information ... use RPI ...' but no evaluation of labeling quality.
Table 4 shows small changes in F1 for ANN-S1/S2 after augmentation.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Estimate noise by sampling FN-augmented examples and measuring mapping and entity-label accuracy; report performance as a function of FN data volume and/or quality filtering threshold.

concerns.title: Choice of MSE for attention loss not justified
concerns.description: Using mean squared error between attention distributions is a design choice; divergences like KL are more standard for distributions and may behave differently—no comparison is provided.
evidence: Section 3.2.2 defines D(θ) as sum squared error between α* and α (Equation 8); no experiments compare loss choices.
Shared analysis flagged MSE vs KL as untested.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report an ablation comparing MSE vs KL divergence vs cross-entropy as attention supervision losses on dev set to justify the chosen objective.

concerns.title: Mechanism specificity: is attention necessary?
concerns.description: Improvements might stem from providing extra supervision about which context tokens matter, but not specifically from attention. Paper does not include such an ablation.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Train a model that receives the same argument-derived signals as explicit features (indicator vectors, pooled argument embeddings) and compare its performance to supervised-attention to determine whether the attention mechanism is the causal factor.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that annotated event arguments—ignored or only indirectly used by existing ED approaches—contain direct, discriminative cues for trigger identification and type classification. To exploit these cues, the authors construct 'gold' attention distributions from ACE argument annotations under two strategies: S1 (attention only on argument tokens) and S2 (gaussian-smoothed attention around arguments). They add an attention-supervision term (MSE between model attention and gold attention, weighted by λ) to the usual cross-entropy loss for trigger classification and jointly optimize both. Experimental evidence on ACE 2005 (specific random split: 529 train, 30 dev, 40 test) shows supervised-attention variants (ANN-S1, ANN-S2) outperform an unsupervised-attention ANN baseline and several prior systems, with ANN-S2 achieving the highest reported F1 in Table 3. They further augment training with automatically-derived FrameNet events (processed to extract core frame elements and automatic entity labels) and report modest additional gains, especially in recall. The paper's reasoning chain is: (1) arguments are informative for disambiguating triggers; (2) supervising attention concentrates model focus on arguments and proximate context; (3) this focused attention yields better representations and classification; (4) additional out-of-corpus event examples can mitigate data sparsity and help attention learning. The manuscript supports these claims with comparative experiments, an analysis of precision/recall trade-offs between S1 and S2, and a modest augmentation study.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that annotated event arguments in ACE 2005 carry useful, often disambiguating information for event detection (ED). It operationalizes this by constructing gold attention vectors from argument annotations and using them to supervise the attention mechanism inside a neural ED classifier. Two strategies are proposed for gold attention: S1 (binary focus only on argument tokens) and S2 (a Gaussian-smoothed attention around arguments to include nearby context). The attention supervision is enforced during training by adding an MSE loss term D(θ) between machine attention α and gold attention α* weighted by λ, producing joint loss J'(θ)=J(θ)+λD(θ). Experiments use a 3-layer ANN with context word/entity embeddings, compare unsupervised-attention baseline (ANN), entity-average attention (ANN-ENT), gold-attention oracle (ANN-Gold1/2), and supervised-attention variants (ANN-S1, ANN-S2). Results on a specific ACE split show ANN-S2 attains best reported F1 (71.7) and ANN-S1 achieves higher precision but lower recall; FrameNet-derived augmentation yields modest additional gains, especially for recall. The authors further hypothesize that prior joint ED+AE methods underperform on ED because of supervision imbalance (many more argument annotations than triggers) and pre-prediction stages that ignore arguments; supervising attention provides a direct path to exploit arguments for ED. The manuscript's reasoning chain: (1) arguments are informative for ED, (2) construct attention targets from arguments (S1/S2), (3) jointly train attention+classifier to align attention to arguments, (4) this alignment yields improved trigger detection/classification, and (5) data augmentation (FrameNet) helps attention learning when ACE alone is sparse. Empirical evidence is provided in Tables 2–4 but key methodological choices (single random split, MSE loss choice, λ settings, and limited statistical details) leave open alternative explanations for the gains.

Node 7: Prior joint ED+AE models underdeliver on ED because of supervision imbalance and pre-prediction practices; supervised attention addresses that by directly channeling argument information into ED (interpretive claim).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes supervising an attention mechanism inside an ANN-based event detector using argument annotations from ACE 2005. Two recipes to build gold attention targets are defined: S1 (binary attention on argument tokens) and S2 (Gaussian-smoothed attention around arguments). The attention supervision is added as an MSE term D(θ) to the classification loss J(θ) with trade-off λ, trained jointly. Experiments on a specific ACE split (529 train, 30 dev, 40 test) show large oracle gains when gold attention is used at test (ANN-Gold1/2), and learned supervised-attention models (ANN-S1, ANN-S2) substantially improve over the unsupervised-attention baseline (ANN) and compare favorably to several prior systems (ANN-S2 reports highest F1=71.7). Augmenting training with automatically derived FrameNet events yields modest further recall/F1 gains. The manuscript's causal chain is: arguments carry disambiguating signal for triggers → construct gold attention from arguments → supervise attention to focus on arguments → improved trigger detection. Evidence in tables supports improved aggregate metrics and a precision/recall trade-off between S1 and S2. However, several key methodological choices (single random split without seed or doc list, MSE vs other divergence choices, λ and S2 parameter sensitivity, potential baseline reimplementation differences, lack of run variance/clear statistical-test protocol, and unquantified noise from FrameNet/RPI processing) leave room for alternative explanations for the gains. I therefore distinguish claims that are well supported by manuscript evidence from those that are only partially supported or overstated, highlight specific uncertainties, and list concrete evaluations that would strengthen causal attribution and reproducibility.

A3: Construct gold attention vectors from annotated arguments (S1 and S2) to encode where the model should focus.
A4: Add MSE attention-loss D(θ) weighted by λ to classification loss J(θ) and train jointly so learned attention aligns with argument-derived gold attention.

A5: If alignment succeeds, learned contextual representations will emphasize argument cues and improve trigger identification/classification (supported by ANN-Gold oracle and ANN-S1/ANN-S2 improvements over baseline).

concerns.title: Causal attribution not isolated: attention supervision vs other uses of arguments
concerns.description: The paper attributes gains to supervised attention, but does not compare to alternative, simpler uses of argument information (e.g., concatenating argument indicator features, multi-task AE supervision, or reweighting losses) to show the mechanism is necessary or superior.
evidence: No controlled comparison to models that incorporate argument features without attention supervision is presented in the evaluation targets or results.
Argument that joint models underuse arguments is not empirically tested with controlled loss-weighting or pre-prediction ablations.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add controlled comparisons: (a) feed argument indicator features/argument-type embeddings directly into the classifier without attention supervision; (b) multi-task AE supervision without attention loss; (c) reweight joint-loss baselines to counter label imbalance. Report whether supervised attention uniquely accounts for gains.

concerns.title: FrameNet augmentation noise and protocol under-specified
concerns.description: FrameNet-derived data are automatically processed via RPI to add entities and limited to core elements, but the noise rate, class mismatches, and mixing strategy with ACE examples are not quantified.
evidence: Section 4.4 describes processing but does not report error rates or quantities (number of FN examples used).
Table 4 shows modest gains but no analysis of how many FN examples contributed or whether gains are due to quantity vs quality.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report the size of the augmented dataset, distribution over event types, estimated noise/error rates from RPI labeling, and experiments varying the amount of FN data to show marginal effect and robustness.

concerns.title: Lack of quantitative attention alignment evaluation
concerns.description: While the paper qualitatively argues attention focuses on arguments, it does not quantify alignment between learned attention and gold attention on held-out data (e.g., attention-AUROC, average KL/MSE), which would strengthen the mechanistic claim.
evidence: No reported metrics that measure how closely learned α matches α* on dev/test (only downstream performance).
ANN-Gold systems (using gold at test) show potential but do not show learned α alignment statistics.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute and report alignment metrics between learned attention and gold attention on dev/test (e.g., average cosine, KL divergence, or precision@k of top-attended tokens being arguments). Correlate alignment scores with instance-level classification outcomes.

alternative_interpretations: Implementation differences (embeddings, tokenization, hyperparameters) could explain part of the baseline gap; supervised-attention models may partly benefit from those implementation choices rather than attention supervision alone.

Gains attributed to attention supervision may instead reflect added supervision signal (argument presence/type features) that could be incorporated more directly (e.g., concatenated features or multi-task losses) without supervising attention.
FrameNet augmentation gains may be due to increased data quantity or more diverse triggers rather than specifically helping attention learning.
transparency_notes: Authors should release dev/test document lists or random seeds and training logs to permit exact reproduction.
Provide per-seed/run metrics (means and standard deviations) and full details of statistical tests to support significance statements.
Detail the FrameNet processing pipeline: counts of examples, mapping table from frames to ACE types, and RPI labeling accuracy estimates (or sample error analysis).

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: Although supervised attention has prior precedents (e.g., Mi et al. 2016), applying argument-derived gold attentions to event detection is a focused, practically novel application. Novelty does not guarantee empirical validity: careful controls are required to attribute gains specifically to attention supervision.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If ACE argument annotations are accurate and predictive of trigger labels, supervised attention should align with discriminative cues and improve ED.
If trained attention reliably approximates gold attention at test time given the model's input features (no gold argument spans), performance gains will transfer to held-out data.

If baseline and prior systems are reimplemented under identical preprocessing and hyperparameter regimes and supervised attention still improves performance across multiple seeds, the claim is robust.

If alternative uses of argument supervision (feature concatenation, multi-task) produce smaller gains than supervised attention in controlled comparison, the attention mechanism is likely the causal driver.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Supervised attention has prior usage; applying argument-derived attention targets to ED is a targeted methodological refinement rather than a radical new paradigm. The S2 Gaussian smoothing choice is borrowed from prior supervised-attention work but adapted to arguments.
evidence: Cited Mi et al. (2016) as inspiration for Gaussian smoothing of supervision.
Paper adapts these ideas specifically to argument supervision in ED with concrete recipes (S1/S2).
uncertainty_flags: Extent of novelty depends on whether prior ED work already used argument-derived features similarly; literature context provided in paper suggests few direct analogs.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Reported F1 gains are substantial relative to baseline and competitive with prior state-of-the-art, but reproducibility and causal isolation issues (split, baseline confounds, lack of variance) reduce confidence in real-world impact until addressed.
evidence: Table 3 shows ANN-S2 F1=71.7 which authors claim is best-in-class.
ANN-Gold oracles indicate argument information can strongly benefit ED if accessible.
uncertainty_flags: Single-split, single-run reporting and baseline differences undermine robustness of the empirical claim.

confidence_interval.rationale: I have moderate confidence that supervised attention using argument-derived gold vectors can improve ED on ACE under the paper's experimental setup (evidence: consistent F1 gains and oracle experiments). However, methodological gaps (single split, unspecified seeds, baseline reimplementation differences, limited ablations and statistical reporting) lower confidence that the result generalizes and that gains are solely due to attention supervision rather than confounding choices. Addressing recommended reproducibility and ablation experiments would tighten the interval.

consensus_findings: The core idea is coherent and plausible: annotated arguments can provide useful, discriminative cues for event-trigger identification and type classification, and supervising attention to focus on argument tokens (or argument-centered context) is a reasonable mechanism to inject that signal.
Oracle experiments (models using gold attention at test) demonstrate that argument-focused attention has the potential to substantially improve ED performance when argument signals are available.

Two gold-attention constructions (S1: argument-only; S2: gaussian-smoothed argument+context) show different empirical behaviors consistent with a precision/recall trade-off in the reported results (S1 higher precision, S2 higher recall).

Augmentation with automatically-derived FrameNet events produced modest additional gains in the reported experiments, particularly for recall, indicating data augmentation can help but that reported improvements are small for the supervised models.

The manuscript lacks several reproducibility and robustness elements that multiple reviewers flagged as necessary to assess empirical claims: exact dataset split (doc IDs/seed), per-run variance (multiple seeds), full statistical-test details, and code/preprocessing release.
disagreements: Magnitude and robustness of reported empirical improvement: some reviewers judged the reported gains (e.g., ANN-S2 F1 = 71.7) likely to be real but dependent on experimental choices; others flagged the ANN baseline as unusually weak and suggested gains may be partially explained by implementation/hyperparameter differences rather than the supervised-attention mechanism itself.

Novelty characterization: some reviewers frame supervised attention for ED as an incremental adaptation of existing supervised-attention ideas (moderate novelty), while others view the explicit use of argument annotations as a more notable conceptual reframing (promising innovation). These views differ in emphasis but do not contradict the factual content of the paper.

Sufficiency of current experiments to make causal claims: one camp feels the provided oracle + learned experiments are a good initial demonstration of mechanism plausibility; another insists that controlled ablations (e.g., injecting the same supervision as features/multi-task rather than as attention) are essential before attributing causal efficacy to attention supervision specifically.
uncertainty_hotspots: Dataset split reproducibility: the paper uses a randomly selected dev/test split (529/30/40) but does not publish the document lists or random seed; this creates uncertainty about comparability to prior work and about result stability across splits.

Statistical testing and run variance: the t-test p-value is reported without specifying number of runs, paired/unpaired setup, or run-level variance; single-run point estimates leave the significance and effect-size uncertainty high.

Baseline strength and implementation confound: the unsupervised-attention ANN baseline performs worse than some published baselines; reviewers are uncertain whether this reflects a genuine limitation of unsupervised attention on ACE or differences in preprocessing, embeddings, optimization, or other implementation choices.

Attention-supervision loss choice and weighting: use of MSE between attention distributions and fixed λ values per strategy is not compared to alternatives (KL, cross-entropy) nor is λ sensitivity thoroughly explored, leaving uncertainty about whether the chosen objective is optimal or robust.
S2 parameter sensitivity: S2 is reported with a single gaussian parameterization (µ=0, σ=1, window=3); the robustness of the precision/recall trade-off to these parameters is untested.

Causal mechanism isolation: uncertainty whether improvements stem from supervising attention specifically or from the extra supervisory signal provided by arguments in any form (e.g., explicit features, multi-task AE supervision).

FrameNet augmentation noise and protocol: mapping FrameNet frames to ACE-like events uses automatic entity labeling (RPI) and core-element selection; noise rates, mapping mismatches, mixing ratios, and their impact on supervised-attention are not quantified.
model_diversity_effects: Reviewers' role specializations drove emphasis and interpretation: the structure/logic analyst emphasized causal chains and logical gaps (calling out oracle vs learned distinctions); methodology auditors foregrounded reproducibility, seeds, and statistical protocol; novelty assessors focused on how the technique relates to prior supervised-attention work and whether adaptation to ED is meaningful; disruptive/creativity lenses highlighted the innovation signal and recommended rigorous validation; claim verifiers compiled evidence-vs-uncertainty lists.

These role-based perspectives collectively increase coverage of evaluation targets: reproducibility and statistical reporting (methodology auditors), causal isolation and ablations (structure analysts and claim verifiers), parameter sensitivity and comparative baselines (novelty and methodology reviewers), and innovation framing (novelty/disruptive reviewers).

Because reviewers focus on different facets, no single reviewer judged the paper fully validated; the diversity of perspectives surfaces complementary verification steps rather than producing a single uniform verdict, increasing epistemic thoroughness but leaving some trade-offs (e.g., novelty vs robustness) unresolved.
meta_review.editor_guidance: As central decision-maker, consider requesting a targeted revision that focuses on empirical robustness and transparency rather than re-framing the conceptual idea. Specifically, ask the authors to (1) release exact ACE train/dev/test document lists or the RNG seed used to create them (and ideally accompanying code to reproduce splits), (2) run all core experiments across multiple random seeds (at least 5) and report mean and standard deviation for P/R/F1, (3) clarify the statistical testing protocol (paired/unpaired test, number of repeats, raw p-values, effect sizes) or use paired bootstrap or permutation tests on per-example outputs, (4) provide code and detailed preprocessing/tokenization instructions so baseline reimplementation confounds can be evaluated, (5) add ablations that isolate the mechanism: (a) same argument supervision injected as non-attention features (indicator/pooled argument embeddings), (b) multi-task AE supervision without attention-loss, and (c) attention-loss alternatives (KL, cross-entropy) and λ sensitivity sweeps, (6) quantify alignment between learned and gold attentions (e.g., average attention mass on argument tokens, KL/cosine metrics, top-k overlap) and correlate alignment with instance-level accuracy, and (7) for FrameNet augmentation, report mapping protocol details, dataset sizes, RPI labeling coverage/estimated error, and experiments varying augmentation amount/quality. These targeted additions address the major reproducibility and causal-interpretation concerns raised by reviewers while preserving the editor's role in judging sufficiency of the revision for further consideration.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen claims and make results reproducible and interpretable, please provide the following in a revision: (1) the exact ACE train/dev/test document identifiers or the random seed and selection script used to produce the reported split; (2) training and evaluation code, gold-attention construction scripts for S1/S2, and FrameNet processing pipeline (including mapping rules and the RPI configuration), or a public repository link; (3) results averaged over multiple random seeds (e.g., 5–10) with mean±std for precision, recall, and F1 for all reported systems (including baselines), and clarification of the statistical test used (paired/unpaired, raw p-values), or adopt paired bootstrap tests on per-example outputs; (4) ablation experiments that isolate the value of supervising attention specifically: a model that receives identical argument supervision as explicit input features or via a multi-task AE objective, and comparison to the supervised-attention variants; (5) ablations comparing attention supervision loss functions (MSE vs KL vs cross-entropy) and sensitivity sweeps for λ and S2 gaussian parameters (µ, σ, window) with a short discussion of stability; (6) quantitative attention-alignment diagnostics on held-out data (e.g., average attention mass on argument tokens, KL or cosine between learned and gold attention, precision@k for argument tokens in top-attended positions) and illustrative examples; (7) detailed description and diagnostic statistics for FrameNet augmentation: number of FN examples used, fraction successfully labeled by RPI, mapping table from frames to ACE types, and an experiment varying FN volume or quality to show marginal benefit; and (8) explicit preprocessing/tokenization and embedding initialization details (so fair baseline comparisons can be performed). These steps will reduce ambiguity about whether reported gains come from the proposed mechanism and will increase reproducibility.

epistemic_limits: This synthesis is limited to the information present in the manuscript and reviewer comments; I cannot inspect the authors' code, rerun experiments, or access the exact data splits used. Consequently, unresolved questions about baseline implementation differences, the impact of specific preprocessing steps, and the numerical stability of hyperparameter choices remain open until authors provide code, seeds, and multiple-run results. Reviewers' assessments are influenced by their role-specific priorities (reproducibility, novelty framing, causal isolation), which can emphasize different failure modes. There is also the broader limitation that ACE 2005 is a single-domain benchmark: even if revisions address concerns on the provided split, generalization to other datasets or languages is not established by the current experiments. Finally, when reviewers infer possible confounds (e.g., baseline weakness or noise in FrameNet mapping), they do so from reported summaries rather than raw outputs, so these inferences are plausible but not definitive.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript proposes supervising neural attention for event detection (ED) by converting ACE argument annotations into gold attention vectors under two schemes (S1: argument-only; S2: gaussian-smoothed argument+context) and adding an attention-alignment loss (MSE weighted by λ) to the trigger classification objective. Experiments on a specific ACE 2005 split (529 train / 30 dev / 40 test) report that supervised-attention variants (ANN-S1/S2) outperform an unsupervised-attention ANN baseline and several prior systems (ANN-S2 reported F1=71.7). Oracle experiments using gold attention at test (ANN-Gold1/2) show large potential gains; augmenting training data with automatically-processed FrameNet examples yields small additional improvements. Reviewers agree the conceptual idea is coherent and promising but raise reproducibility, robustness, and causal-isolation concerns that limit confidence in the reported empirical magnitude and generality.
strengths: Clear, mechanistic hypothesis: argument annotations can be transformed into attention targets and used to guide ED models—operationalized simply as S1/S2 constructions and a joint MSE attention loss.
Oracle (ANN-Gold) experiments empirically demonstrate that argument-focused attention has the potential to materially help trigger detection/classification when argument signals are available.

Reported empirical results show supervised-attention variants outperform an in-paper ANN baseline and several published systems on the stated ACE split; S1 and S2 give an interpretable precision/recall trade-off.
limitations: Reproducibility risk: the paper uses a non-standard randomly selected ACE split (529/30/40) but does not publish the exact document IDs or RNG seed; single-run point estimates (no per-seed means/std) are reported, undermining exact replication and robust comparison to prior work.

Causal attribution under-specified: improvements are attributed to attention supervision, but the manuscript lacks controlled ablations that inject identical argument supervision via alternative mechanisms (e.g., indicator features or multi-task AE losses) to show the effect is attention-specific rather than due to added supervision in general.

Statistical reporting incomplete: a t-test p≤0.05 is mentioned but the number of runs, paired/unpaired test choice, and per-run variance are not given, so significance and effect-size claims are not verifiable.

Design-sensitivity not explored: choice of MSE as the attention divergence, λ weighting values, and S2 gaussian parameters are presented without empirical sensitivity analyses; robustness of results to these design choices is therefore uncertain.
open_questions: Please provide the exact ACE train/dev/test document lists or the RNG seed/selection script used to create the reported split so results can be reproduced exactly.

How stable are the reported P/R/F1 numbers across multiple random seeds (recommend ≥5 runs)? Please report mean±std and clarify the statistical test procedure (paired/unpaired, raw p-values) or adopt paired-bootstrap testing on per-example outputs.

Does providing the same argument supervision as explicit input features (argument-token indicators or pooled argument embeddings) or as a multi-task AE objective yield comparable gains? If so, how does supervised attention compare, isolating attention as the causal mechanism?

Have you compared MSE attention loss to alternative divergences (KL divergence or cross-entropy) and swept λ and S2 gaussian parameters (µ, σ, window)? Please report sensitivity curves (dev set) and justify chosen settings.

Please quantify the FrameNet augmentation pipeline: number of FN examples used, fraction successfully labeled by RPI, mapping table from frames to ACE event types, and estimated label-noise rates. How do ED gains vary with the amount/quality of FN data?

Can you provide quantitative attention-alignment diagnostics on held-out data (e.g., average attention mass on annotated argument tokens, KL/cosine between learned and gold attention, precision@k for argument tokens in top-attended positions) and correlate alignment with instance-level accuracy?
consensus_snapshot: The idea of supervising attention with argument-derived gold distributions is conceptually sound and testable; oracle experiments support the premise that arguments contain useful cues for ED.
S1 and S2 produce different, interpretable precision/recall behaviors; S2 (smoothed context) trades some precision for higher recall and reported best aggregate F1 on the paper's split.

Multiple reviewers emphasize missing reproducibility artifacts (split IDs/seed, code) and missing robustness/statistical analyses (multi-seed results, ablations) as the principal gaps preventing strong empirical conclusions.
disagreement_snapshot: Magnitude and robustness of empirical improvement: some reviewers view the reported gains (e.g., ANN-S2 F1=71.7) as likely meaningful, while others suspect the in-paper ANN baseline is unusually weak and that preprocessing/implementation differences could explain part of the improvement—this remains unresolved without shared code/splits and multi-seed runs.

Novelty framing: reviewers differ on whether this is an incremental application of existing supervised-attention ideas (moderate novelty) or a noteworthy reframing of how AE annotations can be exploited for ED (promising innovation). Both views accept the concept but disagree on how novel it is relative to prior supervised-attention work.
uncertainty_snapshot: Uncertainty about whether reported single-split, single-run improvements will replicate across standard or alternative ACE splits and multiple random seeds.
Uncertainty whether MSE+λ and the specific S2 parameterization are near-optimal or brittle; alternative losses and parameter settings might materially change outcomes.
Uncertainty about the amount and effect of noise introduced by FrameNet→ACE mapping and automatic entity labeling (RPI) and whether augmentation gains are robust to filtering or varying sample sizes.
Uncertainty about mechanism: whether gains are inherently due to attention supervision (as claimed) or simply due to additional supervision signal that could be injected via other, simpler means.

human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript, please provide: (1) exact ACE dev/test document identifiers (or the seed and selection script) and a public code repository containing gold-attention construction (S1/S2), model training/evaluation scripts, and FrameNet processing code (mapping rules and RPI configs); (2) results averaged over multiple random seeds (recommended 5–10) with mean±std for precision, recall, and F1 for all systems reported in tables; (3) exact statistical-test details (paired/unpaired, number of runs) or paired-bootstrap tests on per-example outputs with raw p-values and effect sizes; (4) ablations that inject the same argument supervision via non-attention mechanisms (argument-indicator features, pooled argument embeddings, or a multi-task AE loss) to verify whether attention supervision provides unique benefit; (5) comparisons of attention supervision loss choices (MSE vs KL vs cross-entropy) and λ sweeps plus sensitivity analysis for S2 gaussian parameters (µ, σ, window) with short interpretive discussion; (6) quantitative attention-alignment diagnostics on held-out data (e.g., average attention mass on argument tokens, KL/cosine between learned and gold attention, precision@k of argument tokens among top-attended positions) and illustrative examples; and (7) detailed FrameNet augmentation diagnostics: number and distribution of FN examples, fraction labeled by RPI, mapping table from frames to ACE types, estimated label-noise rates, and experiments varying FN volume/quality to show marginal effects.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary: The paper presents a clear, implementable method to exploit ACE argument annotations by supervising attention (S1 argument-only; S2 gaussian-smoothed argument+context) via an added MSE attention loss. Oracle experiments show argument-focused attention can strongly help ED; learned supervised-attention variants yield reported gains on a particular ACE 2005 split, with S2 achieving the highest reported F1 and S1 favoring precision.
Strengths: Conceptual clarity and simplicity (direct mapping from arguments to attention targets); empirical signals (oracle and learned experiments) supporting feasibility; interpretable trade-off between S1 and S2.
Limitations: Missing reproducibility artifacts (exact split/seed, released code); single-run reporting without per-seed variance or full statistical-test specification; lack of controlled ablations isolating whether benefits are due to attention supervision specifically vs. added supervision in other forms; limited sensitivity analysis for attention-loss choice, λ, and S2 parameters; unquantified noise and protocol details for FrameNet augmentation.
Open Questions: (1) Provide split IDs/seed and multi-seed means±std for core results. (2) How do alternative injections of the same argument supervision (features or multi-task) compare to supervising attention? (3) How sensitive are results to choice of attention divergence (MSE vs KL), λ, and S2 gaussian hyperparameters? (4) What is the FrameNet augmentation quality (counts, RPI labeling coverage/error) and how does ED performance vary with FN data amount/quality? (5) Can you quantify alignment between learned attention and gold attention on held-out data and show correlation with improved instance-level accuracy? (6) Please detail the statistical testing protocol or adopt a paired-bootstrap/permutation test on per-example outputs.
Transparency: Reviewers request code release (gold-attention construction, training/eval scripts, FrameNet processing), exact data split specification, per-seed reporting, hyperparameter search logs for λ and S2, attention-alignment metrics, and FrameNet mapping diagnostics. Addressing these will materially reduce uncertainty and enable reproducibility.

confidence_interval.rationale: Based on reviewer analyses: moderate prior evidence (oracle experiments, consistent direction of learned gains) supports that argument-supervised attention is a promising mechanism. However, substantial uncertainty arises from missing reproducibility artifacts (split/seed/code), single-run reporting, baseline implementation confounds, and absent ablations isolating mechanism. If authors supply requested artifacts and ablations, confidence could move toward the upper bound; absent that, the true generality and magnitude of the effect remain uncertain.
